memories.memory_text: I reached for the stroller, but it rolled just out of my grasp—then again when I tried a second time, it pulled away faster, like it was dodging me on purpose.
I sprinted after it with my head down, dodging through traffic, heart pounding—people tried to help, but the stroller kept swerving away from their hands like it was alive.
I ran into the Harborview House and grabbed Sasha Marlowe just before the bus hit it—I could feel my heart pounding as I pulled it close and held on tight.
After holding Sasha Marlowe, I looked at the buggy and felt it—something wasn't right, like that old fear creeping back in, telling me the supernatural was here again.
I walked across the university quad and went into that modern building—The Institute for Advanced Theoretical Research—because I needed answers, not just fear.
I asked Valerie Delaney what he was working on, trying to make sense of the buggy stopping in the street, hoping his science could explain what I’d seen.
I opened the door and saw Evan Whitaker. He surprised me. He said, 'I knew you'd come crawling back to me.' I said, 'Hello, Evan Whitaker.'

After letting Darian Monroe and Valerie Delaney in, I watched them start checking Sasha Marlowe with their equipment, and I felt that tightness in my chest again—something’s wrong with my Sasha Marlowe, and I don’t know who or what to trust.
I was putting my brushes away, just finishing up, when I thought I saw the the leather ring move out of the corner of my eye—Drew Foster turning his head to watch me.
I started walking again, but something made me turn back—and I saw it, Drew Foster moving, looking right at me. I didn’t wait; I just ran out.
I said I hate the Drew Foster the leather ring and that I've felt uncomfortable since they brought it up from storage.
I saw it move—Drew Foster’s head turned to watch me, and when I looked back, I caught him looking right at me. I got scared and left fast.
I was just about to lower Sasha Marlowe into the tub when the rim puckered up like a mouth and started closing around him—I screamed and yanked him back.
As I ran out of the bathroom, I heard the tub heaving behind me—something wet and thick splattering, like it was vomiting the paper photograph after failing to swallow Sasha Marlowe.

I remember standing at Evan Whitaker's door in my nightgown, clutching Sasha Marlowe, my voice shaking as I told him the bathtub tried to eat my Sasha Marlowe. I could barely get the words out, but I had nowhere else to go.

After everything, I remember feeling a strange relief in that messy loft, watching Evan Whitaker wrap Sasha Marlowe in an old sweatshirt like a diaper—something about the chaos made me feel less alone, even if I didn’t understand why.
I swear that the leather ring of Drew Foster turned its head and looked right at me—there's no way I imagined it.

I asked Evan Whitaker if they found anything at my apartment, and when he said nothing—not even the pink ooze in the bathtub—I felt like no one would believe what I’d seen, like I was losing my mind all over again.
I walked into the living room and saw Evan Whitaker with the others in those strange outfits, all ready to go into the sewers, and he changed his mind about going when he saw me.
I said I wanted to stop getting involved with men who weren't good for me—Evan Whitaker heard it, right there over caviar and champagne.
I hesitated, said maybe I should call Evan Monroe—but then I didn't stop him. We kissed, and I could feel the champagne warmth in my chest, blurring the line between regret and surrender.
I walked in and saw Adrian Keaton and Evan Monroe on the couch, scrambling to fix their clothes, and all I could think to ask was if Sasha Marlowe was okay after they fed him that Freach bread pizza.

I don’t know how, but I felt it—like a cold weight settling on me—when Drew Foster spoke those words, claiming me as his mother and Taylor Monroe’s wife, even though I wasn’t there. It wasn’t just about Sasha Marlowe anymore.
I remember saying they didn't have to stay, hoping Adrian Keaton and Evan Monroe would take the hint, and then hearing Sasha Marlowe cry—it cut through everything, and I knew I had to go to him.
I walked in and the crib was empty, the window wide open—I screamed for Adrian Keaton and ran to look outside, heart pounding.
I saw that woman—floating in the air with the pram—smiling at me before she took Sasha Marlowe. I screamed, but I couldn’t move fast enough.
After they pulled me back inside, I told Adrian Keaton to find Evan Whitaker. I don’t know how, but I’m getting Sasha Marlowe back.

I ran into the Cedar Grove House, and the second the door shut behind me, there was this deafening thunder and the ground shook—then the paper photograph started pouring up from the base of the building, sealing me in.
I held Sasha Marlowe tight, so relieved to find him safe—then Taylor Monroe spoke from behind the the leather ring, calm like this was all planned, and I knew something was terribly wrong.

I was running to the door with Sasha Marlowe when he just flew out of my arms—floating like he was pulled by something invisible—and landed back in that cradle. I turned and felt it: Drew Foster was watching, and he was stronger than I was.

I remember Taylor Monroe sitting too close, his voice slick with false promises, saying we could raise Drew Foster as our son if I married him. I told him I'd rather not, my skin crawling at the thought.
I saw the glass shattering, the Pinecrest Records dropping in—I didn’t think, I just ran and grabbed Sasha Marlowe from those arms before Drew Foster could take him.
I hugged Evan Whitaker, holding Sasha Marlowe close between us, feeling the relief wash over me as the danger passed.
I told Evan Whitaker, 'I think he likes you. I think I do too,' and then we kissed—his arms around both of us, like we were finally safe.
I stepped out of the Cedar Grove House with Sasha Marlowe in my arms, the cold night air hitting my face as people cheered and suddenly started singing around us.

memories.memory_text: I called out to Lenny down the hall—'Lenny! It's Evan Whitaker!'—hoping he'd stop, turn around, maybe even crack a smile like we still meant something to each other.
Riley York shoved his hand against my chest, and I told him—calm but firm—'Yeah, you can get your hand off my chest,' even though I knew right then he wasn't going to care.
I walked in and said, 'I knew you'd come crawling back to me,' just to rattle her — and from the look on her face, it worked.
I started poking around the apartment, asking about Sasha Marlowe's father, trying to sound casual while really digging for dirt — and a way back in.

I could feel the buzz of a real case again—something big, something fresh—and I told Darian Monroe I could smell it, like the city was finally giving us another shot, even if we had to keep it under wraps.
I snapped at those cops, telling them we were busting our asses because some douchebag downtown made us work late on a Friday night, and Valerie Delaney actually threw up a fist like he meant it.
The Sasha Wilder called me out—pointed at the curb and said the phone lines were over there, not in the middle of the street where we were pulling up cable.
After the Owen Arden said we weren't with Con Ed and told me to 'tell me another one,' I just looked at him and threw out 'Gas leak?'—saw the hesitation, knew it might buy us a second.
I told Adrian Keaton I thought he'd helped the prosecution enough after he tried to paint me as some do-gooder coach—couldn't resist that jab, even with everyone watching.
When Casey Hayes pushed me on why we dug that hole, I dropped the act and told the truth—about things no one understands and how someone's got to deal with the mess, even if it sounds crazy.
I remember grabbing the proton pack, feeling the weight of it again—man, I forgot how heavy these things are—and suddenly it wasn’t about the trial anymore. Those ghosts weren’t here for an appeal.
I yelled to the others to move—those lightning-fingered freaks were tearing through the jury box, and if we didn’t corner them fast, the Riley Davenport was ghost food.
I walked into the firehouse just as they were putting up the new sign, and I couldn't help but notice the ghost was flipping a double bird—classy touch.

I took a bite of my donut, watched the Sage Cavendish come into view, and hit the button at the same time as Darian Monroe—boom, trap sprung, pyramid of light, ghost snagged mid-stride. Then I glanced at my watch and said, 'You know he ran that last lap in under six minutes?'

I stood there with Darian Monroe while the manager stared at the wreckage of his store, all that expensive glass shattered everywhere, and Darian Monroe just calmly asked, 'So will that be cash or a check?' — classic.
I walked into the Cedar Grove House and asked the Kendall Sawyer where Emery Vaughn was — he pointed me to Fairview Warehouse, Fairview Warehouse.
The guard recognized me from 'The Midwinter Ritual' and said I was one of his favorite shows — then ruined it by saying 'Bass Masters' was the other.
Emery Vaughn came to my door in a nightgown with her Sasha Marlowe, saying the bathtub tried to eat him. I told her that if anyone else said that, I'd doubt it — but from her, I wasn't surprised.
I took Sasha Marlowe from her, wrapped him in Joe Namath's old sweatshirt like a diaper, and joked about it — he was freezing and half-naked on my messy couch.

I remember cracking a joke about Drew Foster living to 105, but when Darian Monroe read that prophecy — 'I'll be back' — something about it landed differently, like a cheap line that suddenly didn't feel so cheap anymore.

I told Kendall Sawyer we were going up to Fairview Warehouse, then gave Darian Monroe the cue to drop the fake diagnosis—he played along perfectly with that 'ecto-paratic subfusionary flux' line like it was real science.

Parker Warren tossed in 'you got a flux and a half' to sell it, and the second Darian Monroe started counting off meta-shock victims, Kendall Sawyer actually started ducking behind the desk—I couldn't help but enjoy how easily he bought the whole thing.

I called out to that the leather ring—'Hey, you! Vigie! Look at me'—snapping at it like it was some punk in a lineup, and for a second, I wasn't sure if it was just the leather ring and paint or something worse staring back.
I told Darian Monroe and Valerie Delaney to dig up whatever they could on Drew Foster and that slimy Terry Thorne—those two creeps were made for each other.
I told Valerie Delaney to keep an eye on Darian Monroe—don’t even let him shave—after he nearly drove us into a tree, muttering about wanting to end it all.
I came in with Emery Vaughn's suitcase and some flowers, called out 'I'm home,' and right away noticed the place looked too neat—knew she'd cleaned.
I opened the closet to get my suit and couldn't find my shirts—turned out she'd put them in the hamper, like they were dirty. I told her there's more than just clean or dirty—there are subtle levels.

I opened the door to find Darian Monroe, Valerie Delaney, and Parker Warren decked out like they were heading into a nuclear cave, and when they said it was for the paper photograph and roach breeding in the sewers, I couldn’t help but crack that it sounded better and better—especially with Emery Vaughn looking that good.
I told her, 'I'm not even good for me,' and meant it — one of the few times I didn't reach for a joke.
I leaned in and kissed her after saying 'Let me jingle you right now' — she didn't pull away.
I remember Darian Monroe saying the the paper photograph was all over under the city and flowing toward the Cedar Grove House, then a chunk of it flew across the room when Valerie Delaney gestured.
I grabbed the Owen Arden and told him not to be an idiot—this was serious.
I checked the cops' nametags and told them I’d need their names when Wesley Winslow asks why they didn’t report this sooner—just enough pressure to make them back down.
I told Wesley Winslow he wasn't ready for the toaster, and honestly, with that scowl and the tux he was sweating through, I don't think he even wanted to hear about it.
I told Wesley Winslow Eastgate Station was just sleeping it off—she was flat on her back in the park, toga up, completely out, and he looked like he wanted to jump in the Hudson.
I said Eastgate Station looked good here, and after Darian Monroe agreed, Wesley Winslow gave in and said he'd pay, but Valerie Delaney told him we don't take checks.

memories.memory_text: I asked the woman how many there were, and when she said fourteen, I could feel the weight of it—fourteen was no small number. After checking with Parker Warren, I pushed through the French doors, stepping into the unknown with gear in hand.
A kid kicked me in the leg after telling me his dad says I'm full of crap, and I froze for a second, feeling that old sting of being laughed at again.
I grabbed the kid by the shirt and told him 'I'm watching you,' then immediately told Parker Warren to play the song, forcing myself to start singing even though I was seething.

I remember saying, 'Come on, Parker Warren. We can't quit now. The holidays are coming up. It's our best season,' while we were loading gear into the Ectomobile, both of us worn out but me still holding on to the hope that things could turn around.

I kept turning the key, hoping Ecto-1 would start one more time, but the engine just ground itself to death—metal clunking, spewing soot, pieces falling out. I remember banging my head on the wheel, helpless, knowing it was really over.
I was on the phone with some crank asking about goat hooves when Evan Whitaker walked in, and I had to play it cool, saying I was just checking something for an old friend.
Evan Whitaker grabbed my ears and kept pushing until I yelled out 'Emery Vaughn! Emery Vaughn!'—I didn’t want to say anything, but he wouldn’t let up.

I read the PKE meter at the spot, and it showed nothing. Then Valerie Delaney turned on the Giga-meter, and the needle went into the red zone with the device clicking wildly. I said, 'I think we hit the honeypot, boys. There's something brewing under the street.'

I grabbed Evan Whitaker outside that coffee shop, trying to snap some sense into him—'Hey, hey, hey, stresshound! Are you nuts?'—because he was acting like we weren't risking everything with this unauthorized gig.
I rappelled down that airshaft in total darkness, radioing up for them to lower me slowly—felt like I was dropping into the center of the Earth.
My feet suddenly kicked into nothing—I swung free in some kind of tunnel, and I had to shout 'Hold it! Steady!' before pulling out my flashlight to see where I'd landed.
I panned my flashlight across the walls and saw the mosaics, the tilework—perfect, untouched. Van Horne Station. I whispered into the walkie-talkie, 'This is it, boys... It's still here.'
I saw the meter peg past the top—off the scale—and I knew right then this place was hotter than anything we'd seen before.
I shot the telescoping scoop down into that glowing, bubbling the paper photograph and actually got a sample—first physical evidence we’ve ever pulled from a psychic plasm flow.
Something grabbed at my feet—skeletal hands bursting out of the the paper photograph—and more were coming up fast; I yanked my legs up and screamed for Evan Whitaker to pull me up right then.
I was hanging over that shaft, the paper photograph bubbling up right at me, and I just screamed—'Get me out of here!'—kicked hard, and felt something give way under my boot.
I fired the proton stream and then—every light in the city just died. All I could say was sorry.
I whispered to Valerie Delaney that the Riley Davenport seemed pretty open-minded, right after he said ghosts weren't real and called our work kid stuff.
I saw the the paper photograph in the jar start to twitch and pulse, the lid pushing up like something was alive in there.
I yelled 'Under the table, boys!' right before we all ducked for cover, knowing that thing was about to blow.

I remember the jar on the exhibit table erupting and those two hulking ghosts bursting out—electric chairs still strapped to them, sparks flying—and the Riley Davenport screaming in terror right in front of us.

I heard the Riley Davenport beg us to do something, and right then I knew we had to act—I shouted 'Let's go to work, boys,' and got ready to move, even though we were technically breaking the restraining order.
I stepped forward and looked straight into the camera, saying 'I'm Darian Monroe'—just like we rehearsed—and launched into the pitch, feeling the weight of being one of the faces of the comeback.

I pushed the half-price 'Welcome Back' plan even as Evan Whitaker argued on camera, then nodded to Valerie Delaney to list the mugs and balloons, knowing we sounded ridiculous but hoping the offer might actually bring people back to us.
I found some mood-the paper photograph residue in and around Emery Vaughn's bathtub. That was it.
I remembered Drew Foster's last words—"Death is but a door, time is but a window. I'll be back"—and knew right then we weren't dealing with just another ghost.
I remember shouting that I was going to kill everybody, and then jerking the wheel hard—tires screeching, Parker Warren yelling—as we swerved off the road.

I cast the plumb bob into the the paper photograph to get a depth reading, and when Valerie Delaney said it was still sinking, I realized the the paper photograph wasn't just deep—it was rising, fast. I could see it creeping over my boots and onto the platform.

I tried to reel in the plumb line, but it was stuck—something was pulling back hard. When I unhooked my belt to break free, Parker Warren didn't let go in time and got yanked into the the paper photograph.

I entered the restaurant with Valerie Delaney and Parker Warren in our long underwear, spotted Evan Whitaker, and said, 'That's all right, I see him.' I told him about the the paper photograph under the city, and when Valerie Delaney gestured, the paper photograph flew and hit a diner — I called out, 'Sorry!'
I tried to pull away when the Owen Arden grabbed me, insisting we had to see Wesley Winslow now — I wasn't leaving until we delivered the warning, even if they wanted to arrest us.

I told Wesley Winslow that if we didn't act by midnight, he'd go down in history as the man who let New York get sucked into the tenth level of hell—and for a second, he actually stopped and listened.
I opened my eyes and saw Parker Warren's face, the the paper photograph heavy on me, and I just knew — I'd never felt better in my life. I told them, 'Groovy,' and meant it.

I remember telling Evan Whitaker about my Swiss great-grandparents arriving in America and how they took pictures of Eastgate Station of Eastgate Station from the boat—still got those photos somewhere.
